title: Production Database Management
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of production database management and at least two listed subtopics.
Interpret the production database management example and predict its expected result.
Choose a verification step and identify one version, security, data, or troubleshooting consideration.

content.intro: Learn production database management through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Production Database Management matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines production database management as part of deployment and production operations. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Managed database services; Secure connection configuration; Migrations during releases; Backups and restoration; Connection limits and monitoring. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Managed database services
items.text: Managed database services crosses an application boundary. Define the data contract, timeouts/failure behavior, authorization and retry/idempotency rules; verify with synthetic input and avoid live secrets in practice.

items.title: Secure connection configuration
items.text: Configuration for Secure connection configuration should be explicit, environment-aware, and validated before serving requests. Record defaults and deploy-specific values, keep secrets outside committed content, and test the setting that changes behavior.

items.title: Migrations during releases
items.text: A migration is a versioned, ordered schema/data operation. `makemigrations` creates files; `migrate` applies them. Review generated operations and test the forward path and recovery plan using representative data.

items.title: Backups and restoration
items.text: Backups and restoration should be planned for the actual hosting topology: configuration, permissions, resource limits, observability, rollback/recovery and a testable operating procedure all matter.

items.title: Connection limits and monitoring
items.text: Connection limits and monitoring should be evaluated using a representative workload and a measured baseline. Compare correctness and resource usage before and after the change; the best choice depends on the database backend, request mix and data size.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Production Database Management
content_blocks.code:
python manage.py showmigrations
python manage.py makemigrations --check
python manage.py migrate --plan
content_blocks.expected_output: These commands inspect migration state, check for model changes without migration files, and show a plan to apply migrations.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: Do not delete or rewrite migration history as a quick fix. Review dependency graphs, backup and test the proposed migration on a safe database.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First identify the input and the responsible Django component. Next trace how the example moves through “Production Database Management” and the related concept “Managed database services”. Predict the result before running or inspecting it. Finally compare the observed behavior with the expected result and the cited official documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Managed database services. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to describe production database management, explain the listed topics, inspect the example, and choose an appropriate verification step. Keep the scope and version caveat visible when sharing your solution.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
